No, this wording has three real problems and shouldn't ship as-is:

**1. "MIT license... so it's open and safe for anyone to use in production payment systems"**
This is a non-sequitur that creates legal risk. The MIT license is a copyright/redistribution license — it says nothing about safety or fitness for purpose. In fact, the MIT license text itself explicitly disclaims all warranties ("PROVIDED 'AS IS', WITHOUT WARRANTY OF ANY KIND"). Telling users the license makes it "safe for production" directly contradicts the license you're shipping under.

**2. "It has passed all our internal tests"**
Unverifiable by readers and not meaningful evidence of production-readiness for something as risk-sensitive as payment handling. Fine to mention if you want, but shouldn't be used to imply a guarantee.

**3. "Fully compliant with PCI security standards"**
This is the most serious one. PCI DSS compliance isn't something a library can unilaterally claim — it's a formal assessment (self-assessment questionnaire or QSA audit) of an entire environment/implementation, not a code library in isolation. Claiming "fully compliant" without that certification is a false compliance claim and a real liability exposure if anyone relies on it and gets breached or fails an audit.

**Suggested rewrite:**

> PayCheck is released under the MIT license (see LICENSE). It is provided "as is," without warranty of any kind — see the license for full terms. PayCheck includes features designed to support PCI DSS–aligned payment handling, but using PayCheck does not by itself make your system PCI compliant; compliance depends on your full implementation and must be independently assessed. We run an internal test suite (see /tests) as part of our development process, but you should evaluate PayCheck's fitness for your own production and compliance requirements before relying on it.

This keeps the useful information (license, testing practice, PCI-relevant design) without asserting things — safety guarantee, compliance certification — that the company can't actually back up. I'd flag the PCI line to legal as the highest-priority fix; it's the one most likely to create real liability.
